column4: This is the verse behind the section's definition: those who do good receive الْحُسْنَىٰ and an increase, with faces free of gloom and humiliation.
The next ayah supplies al-husna's other face: evil earners receive a matching requital and their faces are covered by abasement and pieces of dark night.
Allah owns all in the heavens and earth so that evil is requited and those who do good are requited بِالْحُسْنَىٰ; this states the section's divine measure exactly.
Dhul-Qarnayn joins faith and right action to جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَىٰ and to an easy command, bringing the section's best outcome, recompense, and ease into one verdict.
Dhul-Qarnayn first assigns punishment to the wrongdoer and a harsher return to his Lord; it is the punitive direction of jazāʾ beside 18:88's beautiful recompense.
After distinguishing those who spend and struggle before and after victory, Allah says وَكُلًّا وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الْحُسْنَىٰ; present giving stands beside the promised best end.
Those who strive with wealth and life exceed those who sit, although وَكُلًّا وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الْحُسْنَىٰ; it directly relates enacted sacrifice, promise, and al-husna.
Those for whom الْحُسْنَىٰ has already gone forth from Allah are kept far from Hell, explicitly making al-husna a prior divine determination of the good end.
The angels meet those spared from Hell with the announcement that this is the day they were promised; it completes 21:101's prior al-husna as a promise now encountered.

People ascribe to Allah what they hate while their tongues falsely claim أَنَّ لَهُمُ الْحُسْنَىٰ; their assigned end is the Fire, matching the section's portrait of treating the best outcome as an entitlement.
The end of those who did evil is السُّوأَىٰ because they denied Allah's signs; it names al-husna's stated opposite and ties that opposite end to enacted denial.
After relief from distress, the self-assured man claims لِي عِنْدَهُ لَلْحُسْنَىٰ even if returned to his Lord; he assumes the promised best without confirming it through giving.
وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضَىٰ reverses the section's roles: here the Lord gives and the recipient reaches the same promised satisfaction.
Garden-reward culminates in رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ, explicitly stating both directions of satisfaction developed in the section.
The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً, holding the servant's satisfaction and the Lord's satisfaction in one return.
فَلِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَىٰ is the near-verbatim counterpart of 92:13: the final and the first belong to Allah.
The command to survey creation leads to ثُمَّ اللَّهُ يُنْشِئُ النَّشْأَةَ الْآخِرَةَ, explicitly identifying the hereafter with the section's “second creation.”
وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ النَّشْأَةَ الْأُخْرَىٰ assigns the other creation to Allah, giving the ontological ground for the promised final recompense.
Those whose best deeds are accepted enter the Garden in fulfillment of وَعْدَ الصِّدْقِ الَّذِي كَانُوا يُوعَدُونَ, an exact scene of the true promise becoming their good end.
A son rejects his parents' promise of being raised, though they tell him إِنَّ وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ; his speech stages the denial of the promised second creation opposite 46:16.
The people of the Garden say they found their Lord's promise true and ask the people of the Fire whether they found theirs true; both directions of the promised end have become experience.
The Garden's inheritors say صَدَقَنَا وَعْدَهُ: Allah has made His promise true and given them the land of the Garden as their settled end.
At resurrection the awakened recognize هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَٰنُ وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ, so the second creation itself verifies the announced promise.
When believers see the confederates they say this is what Allah and His Messenger promised and وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ; the event increases their faith and submission rather than denial.
ثُمَّ صَدَقْنَاهُمُ الْوَعْدَ describes Allah making the promise to His messengers come true through rescue and the destruction of excess-doers.
لَقَدْ صَدَقَ اللَّهُ رَسُولَهُ الرُّؤْيَا states that Allah made the Messenger's vision true in the believers' eventual secure entry, exemplifying the root's realization sense.
Abraham's obedient action is answered with قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ الرُّؤْيَا; conduct, rather than assent alone, makes the announced vision true, just as giving confirms al-husna.
وَلَقَدْ صَدَّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ إِبْلِيسُ ظَنَّهُ is the section's quoted secondary sense: people's following makes Iblis's supposition come true, an ominous counterpart to confirming al-husna.
This definition of righteousness joins belief in the Last Day, giving beloved wealth, and keeping covenants before concluding أُولَٰئِكَ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا; enacted giving displays truth.
Some believers صَدَقُوا مَا عَاهَدُوا اللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ and then fulfill or await fulfillment; endurance and sacrifice embody truth toward what was pledged.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ denies the condemned person both confirmation and prayer; it is the unperformed side of the section's action-based tasdiq.
وَلَٰكِنْ كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ gives the positive description of his refusal, echoing 92:16's exact denial-and-turning pair.
The one who lies about Allah and كَذَّبَ بِالصِّدْقِ when truth arrives embodies the section's act of assigning the promised truth to falsehood.
The one who brings truth and صَدَّقَ بِهِ stands immediately opposite 39:32; the confirmers are identified as the God-fearing.
Those confirmers have whatever they desire عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ, and the ayah calls this جَزَاءُ الْمُحْسِنِينَ, the rightful “with their Lord” counterpart to 41:50's presumption.
Allah removes their worst deeds and rewards them by the best of what they did, completing the confirmation scene with gracious final recompense.
The feeders say إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ and seek neither جَزَاءً nor thanks from people, the closest parallel to 92:19–20's giver without a human return.
They give food, despite loving or needing it, to the poor, orphan, and captive; this supplies the concrete giving whose pure motive 76:9 states.
Because of their patient action Allah requites them with a Garden and silk, showing the otherworldly recompense that replaces the human payment disclaimed in 76:9.
In the Garden they are told إِنَّ هَٰذَا كَانَ لَكُمْ جَزَاءً and that their striving was appreciated, completing giving without earthly return in acknowledged final reward.
Proper spending is only ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ اللَّهِ, and whatever good is spent is repaid in full; it joins the section's exclusive motive to assured recompense.
Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler is assigned to those يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ اللَّهِ, directly matching the giver who seeks only the face of his Lord.
Wealth advanced to grow within people's wealth does not grow with Allah, whereas zakat given seeking His face is multiplied; it tests whether return is sought from people or from God.
Those seeking their Lord's face spend secretly and openly and repel evil with good; their action leads to عُقْبَى الدَّارِ, the good final home.
Allah purchases believers' lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden, calls it a binding promise, and asks who is more faithful to covenant; present surrender trusts the promised return.
Charitable men and women make Allah a good loan that is multiplied, and they receive a noble reward; giving now becomes the act oriented to divine repayment.
The command to spend for one's own good stands against the soul's stinginess, and those protected from it are the successful, closely restaging 92's giver and miser.
A good loan to Allah is multiplied and forgiven, giving 64:16's spender a promised divine return rather than a repayment from a person.
What people possess runs out while what is with Allah remains, and He will reward the steadfast by the best of their deeds; this states why one can give the present away for the final end.
Every small or large expenditure is recorded so that Allah may reward them by the best of what they did, directly linking spending to best final recompense.
People do not attain al-birr until they spend from what they love; the desired good is reached through the concrete surrender of what is presently held.
Those who spend seeking مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ and inner certainty are likened to a fruitful elevated garden; the giving itself seeks divine satisfaction and confirms its return.
Those who spend without following expenditure by reminders or injury have their reward with their Lord, with neither fear nor grief.
Charity spoiled by reminders, injury, and display becomes barren and earns nothing, marking the boundary around the section's giver who seeks only his Lord's face.
هَلْ جَزَاءُ الْإِحْسَانِ إِلَّا الْإِحْسَانُ turns doing good and its beautiful recompense into a compact reciprocal rule.
After promising Gardens and good dwellings, the ayah declares رِضْوَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ; the abundant satisfaction named by the section exceeds even the pictured reward.
On the Day truthfulness benefits the truthful, Gardens are their reward, and رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ completes it with mutual satisfaction.
The foremost believers and their good followers receive mutual satisfaction—رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ—together with prepared Gardens.
Those whose hearts are strengthened with faith receive Gardens before رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ; loyalty enacted in this life ends in two-way satisfaction.
The hereafter contains severe punishment, forgiveness, and رِضْوَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ, setting the two directions of final recompense against the passing play and wealth of worldly life.
Against immediate desires, the God-fearing are promised Gardens, purified spouses, and رِضْوَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ; divine satisfaction is the better thing kept with God.
The follower of God's رضوان cannot be equated with one who returns under wrath to Hell, making divine satisfaction the boundary between opposed final destinations.
The mutually satisfied soul is told to enter the Garden, naming the destination that completes the return of 89:28.
وَلَلْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لَكَ مِنَ الْأُولَىٰ immediately grounds 93:5's promised giving and satisfaction in the final being better than the first.
At the Garden the righteous hear هَٰذَا مَا تُوعَدُونَ, turning a guarded unseen promise into a present welcome.
The Garden's people have whatever they wish and Allah has “more,” closely paralleling al-husna plus ziyāda in 10:26.
Those who believe and do right have Gardens of bliss, so the promised destination follows enacted faith.
Their abiding Garden is وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقًّا, explicitly naming the good end of 31:8 as God's true promise.
إِنَّ وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ is followed by a warning not to let the worldly life or the deceiver delude, the precise choice between trusting the promised end and retaining the near one.
The God-fearing have whatever they wish eternally in the Garden, and it is described as a promise incumbent upon the Lord and asked for.
The God-fearing are promised لَحُسْنَ مَآبٍ, a beautiful final return that expresses the section's “best end” without the noun al-husna.
The transgressors instead have لَشَرَّ مَآبٍ, the evil return that makes 38:49's beautiful end a concrete opposition.
A good deed receives tenfold return while an evil deed is requited only with its like, displaying jazāʾ's two directions and the generosity of the good side.
Whoever brings a good deed receives better than it, while evil-doers are requited only for what they did; the ayah states both directions and a superior good return.
Whoever comes with a good deed receives better than it and security from that Day's terror, a nonlexical picture of the best final outcome.
Whoever comes with an evil deed is cast face-first into the Fire and asked whether the requital is anything but what they did, supplying 27:89's opposite direction.
Whoever seeks worldly reward is told that with Allah are both the reward of this world and of the hereafter, combining the two domains under the one giver of recompense.
بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا identifies preferring the nearer life as the choice opposite giving what is present for the promised end.
وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ supplies the reason for reversing that preference: the final is better and more lasting.
Whoever desires the hereafter and strives for it with its proper striving has that striving appreciated; present action is directed toward and validated by the final end.
أَرَضِيتُمْ بِالْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا مِنَ الْآخِرَةِ rebukes satisfaction with the near life in place of the hereafter, a misplaced رضا opposite the section's final satisfaction.
Wealth and children are adornment of the worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; present holdings are weighed against enduring return.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with Allah is better and lasting; it exposes the mistake of clutching the present gift.
What people are given is worldly enjoyment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting for believers who trust their Lord.
Allah had made His promise true when the believers struck their enemy by His leave; their later faltering marks how conduct affects the experience of an already truthful promise.
After promising believers Gardens, Allah calls His promise true and asks وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ اللَّهِ قِيلًا, answering the implicit charge against the promiser's truthfulness.
The statement that the opponents do not يُكَذِّبُونَكَ but repudiate Allah's signs illuminates the section's dictionary point that takdhīb attaches a speaker or message to falsehood.
Ishmael is called صَادِقَ الْوَعْدِ, a human-side use of the root in which fidelity is shown by fulfilling what one has promised.
إِحْدَى الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ names either victory or martyrdom as one of “the two best outcomes”; unlike the section's Garden sense, al-husna here embraces two hoped-for outcomes.
Iblis had no coercive authority; his realized supposition in 34:20 serves to distinguish one who believes in the hereafter from one in doubt, clarifying how followers make it true.
This ayah supplies 41:50's transition: the person tirelessly asks for good but despairs when harm touches him, before mercy turns into his claim of guaranteed al-husna.
After the boast of 41:50, the human turns away when favored and makes lengthy prayer when harmed, exposing the self-serving posture behind his claimed entitlement.
The resurrection-denier of 46:17 joins earlier doomed communities as the word becomes due against him; the disputed promise thus reaches its adverse direction.
The feeders explain that they fear a grim Day from their Lord, identifying the promised future that governs their present gift.
Allah protects those givers from that Day's evil and grants radiance and joy, beginning the divine answer to their unrepaid act.
يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ identifies the soul addressed by 89:28, making satisfaction part of a completed, tranquil return.
The satisfied soul enters among God's servants before entering the Garden, one step in the return scene surrounding 89:28.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are called the best of creatures, identifying the agents whose Garden and mutual satisfaction 98:8 announces.
The invitation to lend Allah a good loan promises manifold multiplication and places constriction, abundance, and return in God's hands.
Worldly desires and wealth are temporary enjoyment, while وَاللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ حُسْنُ الْمَآبِ; the good return with God prepares 3:15's better promise.
Allah is pleased with believers at the pledge because He knows what is in their hearts, then sends tranquility and near victory; an enacted commitment meets divine رضا.
Knowledge of the first creation is offered as a reminder of the next, complementing the section's use of the hereafter for the second creation.
At the Fire the deniers are told هَٰذَا الَّذِي كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تُكَذِّبُونَ; the promised object they denied has become the scene confronting them.
The people of the Blaze admit that a warner came but they denied and declared the revelation false, showing verbal denial arriving at its warned end.

The one given a good promise and then meeting it is contrasted with one merely furnished with worldly enjoyment before being brought for judgment; this is the section's promised best end versus present possession almost in miniature.
Immediately before al-husna in 10:26, Allah calls to the Abode of Peace and guides to a straight path; it establishes al-husna as the destination of a divine invitation.
In the setting of spending, Satan promises poverty while Allah promises forgiveness and bounty; the giver's act reveals which opposed promise governs him.

Moses asks whether his people were not given a good promise by their Lord and whether they broke their appointment because the wait seemed long; present conduct either holds to or betrays a promised good.
Whoever desires the harvest of the hereafter receives increase in it, while one who desires the worldly harvest receives some of it but no share in the hereafter; action now selects its end.
A human being has only what he strives for, making enacted striving rather than a claimed entitlement the basis of the coming result.
A person's striving will be seen, so the act that confirms or denies an expected end is itself destined for disclosure.
That striving will then be requited with the fullest recompense, extending 53:31's divine measure from good and evil to each person's visible effort.
The Hour is coming so that every soul may be requited for what it strives; this directly joins the second creation, diverse striving, and final jazāʾ.
Every soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, a precise nonlexical formulation of present action making the announced future its own.
Whatever good people advance for themselves will be found with Allah as better and greater in reward, directly locating the return of present giving with God.
Whatever good people advance for themselves they will find with Allah, so the surrendered possession is preserved as a future divine return.
Believers are commanded to spend from God's provision before a day arrives with no trade, friendship, or intercession; giving today answers a specifically announced end.
Believing servants are told to spend secretly and openly before a day comes with neither trade nor friendship, making present generosity the response to a known deadline.
People are commanded to spend before death, when the one who withheld begs for delay so that he may give charity and become righteous; the unrealized gift exposes his earlier choice.
Allah will not delay a soul when its term arrives, closing 63:10's regret and making the time for action irrecoverable.
Those who recite, pray, and spend secretly and openly hope for a commerce that will never perish, recasting present giving as trust in an enduring return.
Allah will pay those spenders their rewards in full and add from His bounty, supplying the promised repayment of 35:29's imperishable commerce.
Those invited to spend include people who withhold, but whoever withholds does so against himself; Allah is the self-sufficient one, reversing the miser's imagined independence.
Those who withhold what Allah gave must not reckon withholding good for them: what they hoarded will encircle them on the Last Day, while the inheritance of all belongs to Allah.
Allah's promise is declared true and unfailing, establishing the reliability that the section's confirmer trusts and its denier rejects.
People know only the outward aspect of worldly life while remaining heedless of the hereafter; this explains the near-sighted posture opposite trusting 30:6's promise.
The God-fearing receive lofty Garden chambers under which rivers flow, followed by the assurance that Allah does not fail the promise.
What people are promised is declared true, directly answering the section's question whether the announced end is truth or falsehood.
The recompense is certain to occur, specifying the event whose promised truth 51:5 asserts.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in it without reduction, showing a return confined to the first life.
Those seekers have only the Fire in the hereafter and their works there collapse, the adverse final side of choosing the present payment in 11:15.
Whoever desires the immediate life receives only what Allah wills and then is assigned Hell; it is the opposite orientation to striving for the hereafter in 17:19.
Allah extends His giving to both the seekers of the immediate and the seekers of the hereafter, so every present gift remains a grant from the Lord.
Worldly differences in divine favor are followed by the statement that the hereafter has greater ranks and distinction, locating the decisive superiority at the end.
People love the immediate life, naming the attachment that makes retaining the present seem preferable to confirming the promised end.
They leave the hereafter behind, completing 75:20's diagnosis as an active abandonment of the final life.
Those opposed to the selfless feeders love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty day, making preference for the present the reason the promised end is neglected.
People are told to seek the home of the hereafter with what Allah has given them and to do good as He did good to them; the present gift becomes the means of the final home.
Whoever lends Allah a good loan is promised multiplication and a noble reward, a compact statement of giving now for divine recompense.
The command not to confer a favor seeking increase can be read as a boundary against giving in expectation of a larger human return, the motive excluded in 92:19.
Charity and other good action done seeking God's satisfaction receive a great reward, joining giving, divine رضا, and promised recompense.
A person sells himself seeking God's satisfaction, expanding the section's surrendered wealth into the surrender of the self for رضا.
A joyous face in the hereafter is satisfied with its striving, linking final رضا directly to the action previously performed.
That satisfied face is in a lofty Garden, specifying the destination in which 88:9's satisfaction is completed.
Disbelievers abide in Hell as the worst of creatures, supplying the direct opposing fate to 98:7–8's best creatures, Garden, and mutual satisfaction.
At judgment a person wishes he had sent something ahead for his true life, a regretful reversal of the giver who already transferred the present into the final end.
Believers who do right receive Gardens as hospitality for what they used to do, making the good destination a requital of enacted faith.
The defiantly disobedient have the Fire and are told to taste what they used to deny, the enacted denial and adverse recompense opposite 32:19.
Creation in truth serves a result in which every soul is requited for what it earned without injustice, stating the neutral two-way scope of jazāʾ.
The believers are given glad tidings of mercy, satisfaction from Allah, and enduring Gardens, placing abundant رضا within the announced good end.
The prosperous garden-owner enters while wronging himself and assumes his present garden will never perish, grounding his false confidence in what he currently holds.
He doubts the Hour yet claims that, even if returned to his Lord, he will find a better resort; this closely parallels 41:50's unsupported claim to al-husna.
Praise belongs to Allah in the first life and the hereafter, judgment belongs to Him, and all return to Him; both domains and final verdict remain His.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making even the smallest present act meet its final disclosure.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, supplying the equal adverse direction beside 99:7's good act.
Those who say their Lord sent good are told that good-doers have good here and that the home of the hereafter is better, joining received truth, conduct, and the best home.
Everlasting Gardens are the destination of the God-fearing and contain what they desire, making concrete the better final home announced in 16:30.
Wealth and children are a trial while a tremendous reward is with Allah, preparing 64:16–17's command to overcome stinginess and spend.
Allah expands and restricts provision and replaces whatever people spend; the provider Himself guarantees the giver's return.
Some believers treat what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and the Messenger's prayers, and Allah promises to admit them into His mercy.
